newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook - Markets to resume advances.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook - Markets to resume advances.

text.p: Non-ferrous metal prices look set to resume a new year rally that was temporarily halted last Friday on the London Metal Exchange (LME), traders said.
Copper and aluminium stalled at technical resistance levels on Friday, but remain nicely placed to push higher once more.
"Copper is very tight at the moment, and some of the tightest dates are coming up shortly," one trader said.
Aluminium bulls are looking for that market to build a bridgehead above the $1,600 level a tonne again.

"Producers have been selling around there ($1,600), but that's OK. They don't want the market to run away with itself. Once the consumers chip in, the funds could take it on as well," another trader said.
Copper prices ended Friday's LME session at $2,255, but after another spell of consolidation are expected to chase up and challenge initial resistance at $2,280 and then the recent peak of $2,313.
The cash/threes backwardation firmed to $160/170 after finishing at a strong $150 on Friday, with Jan/February now showing a $100 premium.

Stock movements will be important following Friday's 3,425-tonne decline in LME warehouse inventories. Further drawdowns are likely once physical demand in the first quarter -- traditionally the busiest period -- picks up.
In aluminium, inventory data last week was mixed, with LME stocks rising, while the IPAI reported falling producer stocks.
Producer stocks fell 33,000 tonnes to 1.653 million tonnes, the lowest since November 1992, while fabricated inventories of 1.437 million tonnes are the lowest for over 15 years.
Analyst Nick Moore of the Flemings Global Mining Group noted that although there has been an element of re-distribution producer stocks have fallen more than LME inventories have risen recently.
"It (the data) not only supports current prices, but it opens the door for better prices as the hedge funds move in," he said.
Macquarie Equities said that if LME stock increases were to continue the market would become nervous, but there were encouraging signals coming from the U.S., where physical premiums are picking up.

"U.S. premiums are now approaching the levels which would justify shipping material from European warehouses, offering the prospect of a pick-up in withdrawals from LME warehouses in the coming weeks," Macquarie said.
The rest of the metals complex was likely to take its cue from copper, with nickel in particular also set to resume its 1997 advance and head for a test of $7,450, traders said.
